result:
If you look up at the night sky and find the faint smudge of the Andromeda galaxy, the light hitting your eyes left its source about two and a half million years ago. When those photons began their journey across the void, early hominids on Earth were just figuring out how to strike one stone against another to make a sharp edge. 

In a very real sense, there is no universal "now." Looking out into space is only ever looking backward in time. Every star is a ghost; every galaxy is a memory.

We humans are obsessed with leaving a mark, with fighting the inevitable march of time. It is perhaps our most defining trait. And if you want to see the purest distillation of that defiance, you don’t need to look at great pyramids or towering skyscrapers. You just need to look at two pieces of gold-plated copper currently hurtling through the freezing dark of interstellar space.

In 1977, we launched the Voyager 1 and 2 probes. On the side of each, we bolted a phonograph record. 

Inside that golden shell, curated by a committee led by Carl Sagan, we packed a summary of our world. We included the sounds of surf, wind, and thunder. We included the songs of humpback whales and the chirping of frogs. We recorded greetings in fifty-five languages, starting with Akkadian, a language that hadn't been spoken for millennia, and ending with Wu, a modern Chinese dialect. We included Bach, Mozart, Blind Willie Johnson, and Chuck Berry’s "Johnny B. Goode." 

We even included the recorded brainwaves of a young woman named Ann Druyan, who, while hooked up to the sensors, meditated on the history of Earth and the intense, dizzying feeling of having just fallen in love. 

Think about the audacity of that. And the unbearable, beautiful optimism of it. 

The universe is incomprehensibly vast, mostly empty, and entirely indifferent to our existence. The chances of an extraterrestrial civilization actually intercepting one of the Voyager probes in the fathomless dark of the cosmos are practically zero. The space between stars is simply too big, and the probes are too small. 

Which means we didn't really make the Golden Record for the aliens. We made it for ourselves. 

In the midst of the Cold War, while humanity had thousands of nuclear missiles pointed at its own head, a small group of people sat in a room and asked: *If we have to introduce ourselves to the cosmos, who do we want to be?* 

We chose to be the species that listens to the rain. We chose to be the species that makes intricate music, that marvels at geometry, that falls in love. We left out the wars, the famines, the cruelty, and the fear. Was it a dishonest portrait? Maybe a little. It was certainly curated. Like anyone putting together a photo album, we chose the pictures where we were smiling. 

Billions of years from now, long after the Earth has been swallowed by an expanding, dying Sun, those two Voyager probes will likely still be drifting through the Milky Way. The continents we stood on will be vaporized. Every monument we built, every war we fought, every poem we wrote on paper will be gone. 

All that will remain of us are those two tiny time capsules, silently carrying the sound of a human heartbeat, a mother kissing her child, and the sliding steel guitar of Blind Willie Johnson humming *Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground* into the endless, velvet quiet. 

I find a strange, profound comfort in that. It means that no matter what happens to us down here, the best parts of who we were have already escaped. We threw a message in a bottle into the cosmic ocean, and in doing so, we whispered to the universe—and to ourselves—*We were here. And for a little while, it was wonderful.*
